$comment: One answer per (comparator, field, value, subscriber), executed by BOTH
segment engines: the SQL compiler in apps/api/internal/segments and the
This file exists because the two engines answered the same user-visible
question differently. A flow branch reading `Tag contains vip` took the
false leg for a subscriber tagged `vip-gold`, while the identically-worded
segment matched them — the SQL side compiles `contains` to ILIKE '%vip%'
and the Go side compared tags for exact equality. Worse, the Go evaluator
recognised `eq`/`neq` while the SQL compiler emits `equals`/`not_equals`,
so a condition authored through the segment vocabulary fell through to a
silent `return false` and routed 100% of traffic down the false leg with
Two implementations validated on their own side are not one contract. A
row added here must be answered identically by both, or one of them fails.
`skip_sql` marks rows the SQL engine cannot express against a real column
(tag-array semantics live in a different compiler path); those rows still
bind the Go evaluator. Nothing is skipped for the Go side.

cases.name: equals is the canonical spelling and both engines honour it
cases.why: The Go evaluator recognised only `eq` and fell through to a silent false.

cases.name: eq is accepted as an alias, not a second vocabulary
not_equals is the canonical spelling
contains on a string is a substring match, not equality
contains is case-insensitive, matching ILIKE
cases.why: SQL compiles to ILIKE; Go used strings.Contains, which is case-sensitive.

cases.name: contains on a tag list matches a substring of any tag
cases.why: The headline case. `vip-gold` matched the segment and failed the identically-worded flow branch.

cases.name: contains on a tag list still does not match an unrelated tag
not_contains is the exact negation of contains
starts_with exists in both engines
cases.why: The Go evaluator had no starts_with at all — it returned a silent false.

cases.name: starts_with is anchored, not a substring
ends_with exists in both engines
is_not_null is the canonical spelling of exists
is_null is the canonical spelling of not_exists
numeric gt compares numbers, not strings
numeric lte is inclusive
in matches when the value is one of the list
cases.why: `in` is declared by the shared vocabulary and compiled by the SQL engine, but was missing from the flow evaluator's comparator map — so it fell through to a silent false and routed 100% of subscribers down the FALSE leg.

cases.name: in does not match when the value is absent from the list
cases.why: The negative case, so a stub returning true for every `in` cannot pass.

cases.name: not_in is the exact negation of in
cases.why: Paired with the case above; both engines must agree on the negation, not just the positive.

cases.name: not_in does not match when the value IS in the list
cases.why: Guards the negation against a stub that always returns true.

cases.name: in over an empty list matches nobody
cases.why: SQL compiles `IN ()` to FALSE (compile.go). Membership of nothing is false, and an evaluator that treated an empty list as 'no filter' would match everybody.

cases.name: not_in over an empty list matches everybody
cases.why: SQL compiles `NOT IN ()` to TRUE. The asymmetric half of the empty-list rule — the one an implementation is most likely to get backwards.

cases.name: lt is strict at the boundary
cases.why: `lt` had no parity case at all. The boundary is where a `<` / `<=` mix-up shows, and nowhere else.

cases.name: gte includes the boundary
cases.why: `gte` had no parity case. Same boundary, opposite inclusivity — together lt/gte pin both sides of it.
